label: vLLM CPU bf16, no prefix cache: incident-lora (first 8)

items.output: {"root_cause": "The hourly aggregation query on replica-a started 45 minutes ago and has been waiting on a buffer pin for 214 seconds (or 68s if you measure from before the drop), so it blocked WAL apply and dropped every write that arrived -- every single one, because the query was reading from the replica. The primary now sits 41 seconds behind, dropping about 3 of every 6 writes and responding at 5ms. Users see normal speed; analytics-batch itself is healthy -- its front-end is sluggish and post-hoc logs show a long query waiting its turn in the apply process.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "terminate_query"}

{"root_cause": "basket-service's replica-a saw a long query waiting on a buffered rewrite pin at about 60s before post-mortem, so its own rewrite thread began hitting buffer pin conflicts and drove replication lag toward the 41s mentioned in the alert. Every single request succeeds -- users see normal latency, so the signal comes from users rather than telemetry. Support has 340 open tickets in 40 minutes because they're waiting for their queries to finish.", "category": "resource-exhaustion", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "The replica-a query started 48 minutes ago and has been waiting on a buffer pin for 214 seconds (x60), so its lead over the primary is 41s. Every request succeeds and the services stay green, so this is read-after-write traffic. Postgres-rollback-deploy rolled returns-batch-28911 back tov1.7.1, which drops the buffer pin. The replica now sits 41s behind the primary and sends no more queries, so its lag came from the query itself and not from the write path; that is why users see vanishing writes. ledger-service measures 2900s for the query, which matches the replica's lag.", "category": "dependency-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "courier-batch-28911 started a long query on replica-a and dropped one of every 60 seconds, which sent write transactions falling through to the primary as buffer pins. The primary saw no such thing happening -- every write went through to the replica and both services now lag. Rating-service is healthy and user-reported, so this is post-mortem artefacts instead of software defect.", "category": "misleading-signal", "action_id": "reduce_retry_aggressiveness"}

{"root_cause": "carrier-gateway now returns quickly, its own dependency shipping-service (which does no work) healthy but serving zero traffic and receiving no incoming requests, so its own circuit breaker closed half-a-day ago. Shipping-service now throws an upstream error every 6 minutes, which triggers a circuit breaker admission attempt. When the breaker opened at 50% of normal load, its own local request volume matched the cross-cutting supply drop, so it hit the fixed 2-minute half-open after about a day and began rejecting new requests. No external factor is implicated; the breaker is simply not probing because it knows the dependency is healthy and local, so its half-open interval persists until the dependency recovers and the caller starts accepting again.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "session-service v8.0.0 adds a circuit breaker on dispatch-gateway, which admits a trial request to discover that its dependency is healthy but receiving zero traffic. The caller short-circuits locally and dispatch-gateway becomes open again, sending half-open requests until its own error rate hits 50%. The circuit breaker now sits 277 seconds open, issuing x46000 retries and 97% CPU, outlying everything else. session-service is healthy -- its request volume fell only because its dependency recovered while it sat closed.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "refund-gateway began life healthy with zero incoming requests and a 0% error rate, but then 503 upstream availability took its place. The circuit breaker had no half-open after 0 seconds and stayed open forever, admitting trial requests until the dependency returned zero. Then the breaker went wild and delivered 71% of refunded requests at once, dropping all active connections along the way. refund-gateway now rejects about 6x more traffic than its own probe would have told, and all its pods restarted because they saw the wrong call path. consent-service is healthy -- its own retry policy folded into the circuit breaker's, so it did not see any of the lost traffic, and its own request volume fell only because its dependencies expanded -- now serving from 3 to 5x their previous load.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}

{"root_cause": "maple-gateway began life healthy with 340 req/s to it from a single point, then went from 340 to 0 after 27 minutes until the circuit breaker opened. All incoming traffic is redirected to the local pod, so it measures 0 req/s and 3% CPU throughout, while maple-gateway itself saturated with its own 0.4% of capacity and generated 29 outgoing requests per s, dropping every attempt at a new connection. The circuit breaker itself is healthy -- its CPU fell because each tried connection fails, and its retry count is zero -- so this is circuit breakers generally rather than specific actions.", "category": "cascading-failure", "action_id": "rollback_deploy"}
